update description: Specify Needs phase activities are increasingly supported by automation and AI for synthesizing and structuring stakeholder inputs, analyzing options, and drafting business case materials. Routine and repetitive aspects of needs identification, consultation, and documentation are reduced, shifting staff effort toward contextual interpretation, prioritization, validation, and strategic decision-making.
interdependencies: Impacts later methodological recommendation work by changing how user needs and feedback are gathered and validated before improvements to collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation are proposed.

Impacts data/user support activities because external and internal user requests will increasingly arrive pre-structured through automated intake, requiring validation and contextual interpretation rather than manual triage.
impact reasoning: For the EC-02 Economist/Sociologist 2, the Specify Needs update changes the front end of analytical and consultation work from manually gathering, organizing, and summarizing stakeholder input toward working with AI-assisted needs identification outputs. The role remains guided and supportive, but expectations shift toward validating machine-generated summaries of user requirements, identifying gaps or biases in automated interpretations, translating nuanced subject-matter context into usable specifications, and helping refine recommendations based on prioritized needs. This alters the position from primarily participating in downstream analysis after needs are already articulated to playing a more active quality-assurance and contextualization role in how needs are initially framed. The role will also need to understand the strengths and limits of automated consultation and drafting tools so that recommendations for survey and program improvements are based on reliable and representative inputs.

update description: This sub-process includes the initial investigation and identification of what statistics are needed and what is needed of the statistics. In the modern process, AI and automated tools are used to continuously scan for new information requests from users, detect relevant environmental changes, and aggregate respondent feedback and evaluation action plans. These technologies also benchmark needs by automatically referencing practices among other (national and international) statistical organizations. Automation supports the collation, analysis, and structuring of these triggers for new or changed statistics, while staff focus their expertise on interpreting context, confirming significance, and ensuring response to complex or emergent requirements.
interdependencies: Potential downstream effects on later survey/methods review work because AI-supported needs identification will shape recommendations for collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods.

Potential downstream effects on subject-matter studies and project planning because automated benchmarking and feedback synthesis will influence priorities, target dates and scope of analytical reviews.
impact reasoning: For the EC-02 Economist/Sociologist 2, the main change is not full ownership of automated needs identification, but participation in an environment where early-stage needs assessment is increasingly AI-enabled. Work that currently emphasizes under-guidance participation in analysis, trend identification, user support, and methodological feedback will shift from more manual scanning and collation of user requests, respondent feedback, and environmental signals toward validating, interpreting, and contextualizing AI-generated signals and benchmarks. The role will need to assess whether automatically surfaced needs are statistically meaningful, methodologically feasible, and aligned with program context, legal obligations, and organizational priorities. This increases the importance of critical review of automated outputs, data/metadata literacy, and the ability to translate AI-supported findings into recommendations for survey or program improvements. The updated work-description would differ from its current state by adding routine interaction with automated monitoring and benchmarking tools, greater responsibility for judging the relevance and quality of machine-generated need signals, and stronger emphasis on contextual interpretation rather than only manual information gathering.

Analytical material will increasingly need to explain not just statistical findings, but also the rationale for accepting, rejecting, or prioritizing machine-identified needs.

update description: This sub-process systematically checks whether current sources of data could meet user requirements and the conditions under which they would be available, including any restrictions on their use. Existing data holdings must be exhaustively investigated and prioritized first, followed by a search for relevant administrative and alternative data sources; the option to conduct new surveys is only considered if these avenues prove insufficient to meet data needs. The subject matter sponsor holds sole accountability for certifying that all relevant avenues for data have been thoroughly explored and that the suitability, timeliness, and quality of any proposed source have been rigorously assessed. To expedite and strengthen the acquisition of administrative and alternative data, a center of expertise works collaboratively with subject matter specialists to support negotiations, acquisition logistics, and the establishment of legal or operational agreements where needed. When multiple avenues have been assessed and documented, a strategy for filling any remaining gaps is prepared. This sub-process also encompasses the assessment and possible updates to the legal framework for data collection, ensuring fit-for-purpose, respondent-efficient, and timely data acquisition and usage.
interdependencies: Cross-functional legal, privacy, and data acquisition support processes
impact reasoning: The work-description shifts from participating in analysis of already-collected program data and suggesting improvements to collection and processing methods, toward a more structured upstream role in assessing whether data needs can be met through existing holdings, administrative data, and alternative data before proposing new survey activity. For the Economist/Sociologist 2, this means a stronger expectation to support systematic source discovery, comparability assessment, documentation of source suitability, and evidence-based recommendations on source hierarchy. Although sole certification accountability sits with the subject matter sponsor, this position will contribute substantially to the analytical groundwork used for that certification. The role will also need to work more routinely with a center of expertise on data acquisition, legal/operational agreements, and feasibility constraints. Compared with the current state, the updated work-description would differ by placing greater emphasis on source inventorying, administrative/alternative data fitness assessment, legal and operational usability considerations, metadata and quality review, and documented gap analysis before recommending collection changes or survey development.

update description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase in the form of a business case to get approval to implement a new or modified statistical business process. In the contemporary process, automated and AI-driven systems are used to collate, analyze, and generate initial drafts for all key business case sections—including the description of the 'As-Is' process, the proposed 'To-Be' solution, and the relevant assessments of cost, benefit, risks, deliverables, and impact. Staff and sponsors then review, contextualize, and refine these drafts, ensuring proper alignment with strategic objectives and organizational needs before final submission. The business case is reviewed and approved by the relevant body, with human expertise providing the final evaluation and decision. By leveraging automation, the preparation of business cases gains efficiency and speed, allowing human effort to be concentrated on strategic oversight and quality assurance.
interdependencies: Upstream findings from earlier phase 1 sub-processes become machine-collated inputs for the business case, increasing the need for consistent documentation and traceability.

Outputs from 1.6 shape downstream design and implementation decisions through the approved 'go/no go' recommendation, so weaknesses in human review of AI-generated drafts may propagate into later phases.
impact reasoning: For the Economist/Sociologist 2 role, the update shifts contribution to business-case preparation from mainly supporting analysis and recommendations under guidance to also reviewing, validating, contextualizing, and refining AI-generated business-case content. The role remains junior/supporting, but expectations increase for assessing whether automated drafts accurately reflect statistical program realities, methodological implications, stakeholder considerations, and operational constraints. The work-description would differ by placing greater emphasis on strategic quality assurance of machine-prepared material, traceability of evidence used in recommendations, and clearer articulation of risks, costs, benefits, and program impacts in forms suitable for approval processes. This adds a new layer of digital review responsibility without removing the need for subject-matter analysis.

update description: This phase describes the development and design activities, and any associated practical research work needed to define the statistical outputs, variables, methodologies, collection instruments, and operational processes—with a strong emphasis on automation, AI-powered tools, and digital interoperability. Automated and AI-driven processes play a central role in drafting specifications, aligning with corporate and international standards, generating and enriching metadata, simulating system interactions, and iterating design improvements. All statistical products and their supporting metadata are produced in standardized, richly described, and machine-actionable forms, ensuring they are interoperable and reusable across downstream tools, APIs, and organizational systems. Staff are freed from repetitive and routine design work and instead focus on innovation, calibration, and optimizing for evolving user and stakeholder requirements. Design activities thus promote efficiency, quality, and discoverability, embedding best practices for automation, standardization, and open data access. The Design phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 8), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, can occur in parallel, and may be iterative. Iteration between Design and Build phases is supported through automated versioning and process enhancements.
impact reasoning: For the EC-02 Economist/Sociologist 2, the Design phase update shifts part of the role from contributing feedback on methods and procedures in largely manual or document-based ways to participating in digitally enabled, standards-based, and metadata-driven design work. Under guidance, the position would increasingly review AI-assisted specifications, assess whether automated design outputs reflect subject-matter needs, and help ensure that methodological choices, variables, concepts, and output structures remain analytically valid and usable. The role remains developmental and support-oriented, but expectations expand to include understanding machine-actionable metadata, interoperability requirements, automated versioning, and the implications of digital design choices for downstream collection, processing, analysis, and dissemination. Routine drafting and formatting work would decrease, while evaluative, translational, and quality-oriented contributions would increase. This also implies a stronger role in communicating subject-matter requirements into structured design specifications and in identifying risks where automation may reduce methodological fit, interpretability, or coherence.

update description: This sub-process designs the statistical methodology to be applied during the Process and Analyse phases, with a core emphasis on standards-based automation, AI enablement, and digital interoperability. Specifications for routines and rules covering coding, editing, imputation, validation, and data integration/estimation are required to be implemented, where practical, using automated frameworks and AI/ML-driven tools—leveraging SDMX models, .STAT processing, and corporate-standard solutions (e.g., Aria/Colectica). Human analysts and methodologists are focused on reviewing and updating analytic methods for non-standard or novel use-cases, with all standardizable and repeatable components digital, automated, and reproducible by default. Statistical disclosure control and quality assurance methods designed here also leverage automation and AI for rapid, secure, and scalable deployment. All methodologies are documented to be compatible with downstream digital workflows and to support auditing, versioning, and continuous improvement.

impact reasoning: The current EC-02 work-description emphasizes participation under guidance in analysis, methodological review, and feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation, and presentation methods. Update 2.5 shifts this role from primarily reviewing and suggesting improvements to increasingly operating within a methodology design environment where standard processing and analysis rules are expected to be automated, metadata-driven, interoperable, and reproducible by default. For this position, the practical effect is not full ownership of enterprise architecture or advanced methodological design, but a stronger expectation to assess whether analytical routines, validation checks, estimation approaches, and quality/disclosure controls can be expressed in corporate-standard, machine-actionable forms and reviewed within AI-enabled processing pipelines. The role evolves toward validating the theoretical appropriateness of automated methods, contributing subject-matter input to standardized rule design, identifying cases where standard automation is insufficient, and documenting decisions so they support downstream audit, versioning, reuse, and continuous improvement. This also changes the balance of effort: less manual bespoke handling of recurring analytical tasks, and more structured review of automated outputs, metadata specifications, and standards compliance. Future role evolution would likely include greater contribution to the governance of AI-assisted methodological components and to the translation of subject-matter needs into reusable digital processing specifications.

update description: In this phase, statistical outputs are produced and examined in detail using automated, AI-powered, and modular analytical pipelines. All workflows—from draft output and commentary preparation to validation and finalization—leverage digital automation and AI/ML-driven solutions, producing real-time, reproducible, and version-controlled results. Automated generation of daily write-ups, dashboards, and other standardized products is the norm, with human analysts focused on interpretation, contextualization, and providing tailored, nuanced analysis for users. Intelligent, real-time validation and anomaly detection are embedded throughout. The phase is fully iterative and feedback-driven, supporting rapid, responsive, and continuous analytic enhancement. The Analyse phase and its sub-processes are applicable to all outputs regardless of data source, and support the seamless transition to dissemination.

Creates downstream impacts on dissemination activities through increased use of automated commentary, dashboards, and tailored user-facing analytical products

impact reasoning: This update materially changes the EC-02 Economist/Sociologist 2 role from primarily participating in analyst-led statistical examination and preparation of analytical material to operating within automated and AI-supported analytical environments. The position will spend less time on manual production of routine outputs and more time reviewing AI-generated analyses, interpreting findings in subject-matter context, assessing whether automated outputs are credible and fit for purpose, explaining limitations, and tailoring analytical products for internal and external users. The role's contribution to trend identification will increasingly rely on interacting with dashboards, anomaly alerts, and reproducible pipelines rather than ad hoc manual analysis. The position will also need to understand version-controlled analytical workflows, embedded validation rules, and the implications of AI/ML-assisted commentary generation. Operationally, this means stronger responsibilities for quality assurance of automated outputs, documenting interpretive choices, and using iterative feedback from analysis to recommend improvements to earlier production stages. Over time, the role evolves toward a hybrid analyst-steward function: validating automated outputs, contextualizing them for users, and contributing to continuous enhancement of analytical pipelines and methods.

update description: This sub-process transforms processed and finalized data into statistical outputs using automated, AI-powered pipelines. Outputs—including indices, seasonally adjusted statistics, mapped data, geo-statistical services, write-ups, dashboards, and methodological documentation—are generated by default through LLM/AI-driven automation. Human analysts intervene to interpret, refine, or tailor outputs for specialized, complex, or critical communication needs. AI-generated methodological notes and narratives accompany all outputs, documenting analytic approaches and logic. This automation-first approach maximizes efficiency, consistency, and allows analysts to focus on providing added value and insight.
impact reasoning: The current EC-02 work-description assumes that the incumbent participates under guidance in analysis and assists in preparing analytical material, largely through conventional analyst-driven production. Under update 6.1, draft outputs, narratives, dashboards, and methodological notes are produced by default through AI-enabled pipelines. This shifts the role away from primarily manual preparation of outputs toward review, interpretation, quality assurance, contextualization, and tailoring of automated products for internal and external users. Update 6.3 changes the nature of this work from primarily human-authored interpretation toward a human-in-the-loop model in which AI tools generate initial narratives, explanations, and visualizations that must be critically reviewed, corrected, contextualized, and tailored for different audiences. For the Economist/Sociologist 2 level, this means greater responsibility for validating AI-generated interpretations against statistical evidence, methodological context, and subject-matter knowledge, while still operating under guidance for more complex or sensitive outputs. The role shifts from only assisting with analytical interpretation to also evaluating the quality, limitations, and appropriateness of automated explanations and ensuring that outputs remain accurate, policy-neutral, comprehensible, and aligned with confidentiality and organizational standards. This update also implies more frequent use of AI-assisted analytical and communication tools, requiring stronger judgment in distinguishing plausible automated summaries from analytically sound interpretations.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of statistical program data and assists in the preparation of analytical material for internal use and publication purposes.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This activity expands from assisting with conventional analytical material to reviewing and refining AI-generated first-draft narratives, summaries, and visual explanations. The employee would need to check whether automated interpretations accurately reflect the data, methods, caveats, and intended audience, and then improve clarity and contextual relevance before internal or public use.

gaps.justification: The current work-description emphasizes participation in analysis and preparation of analytical material, but does not require capability to assess machine-generated interpretations for factual accuracy, bias, omissions, or overstatement.
gaps.name: AI-assisted analytical review
gaps.description: Ability to critically assess, edit, and refine AI-generated narratives, summaries, and visual explanations so they accurately reflect statistical findings and methodological limitations.

gaps.justification: The update introduces automated first-draft explanations and visualization outputs, which requires understanding of how AI tools generate narrative and analytical suggestions and where they may fail.
gaps.name: Operational understanding of LLM/AI output limitations
gaps.description: Knowledge of common failure modes of LLM/AI tools, including hallucinations, unsupported causal inferences, missing caveats, misleading emphasis, and inconsistency with source outputs.

gaps.justification: The updated process requires making results accessible and meaningful for varied audiences, beyond technical internal preparation alone.
gaps.name: Audience-adapted statistical communication
gaps.description: Ability to tailor AI-assisted and human-authored explanations of statistical outputs to technical and non-technical audiences while preserving analytical precision.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Identifies statistical trends and developments.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Trend identification will increasingly be supported by automated analytics and AI-generated explanatory cues. The role now includes judging whether machine-suggested trends, drivers, or comparisons are statistically credible and substantively meaningful, rather than accepting automated pattern descriptions at face value.

gaps.justification: The current requirement covers trend identification, but not the evaluation of machine-generated pattern detection or explanatory statements.
gaps.name: Validation of automated trend interpretation
gaps.description: Ability to verify whether AI-identified trends, anomalies, and explanatory patterns are supported by the underlying data, definitions, and production context.

gaps.justification: AI-generated explanations may blur descriptive, correlational, and causal interpretation; the role will need stronger discipline in distinguishing these forms of inference.
gaps.name: Inference literacy in AI-supported analysis
gaps.description: Knowledge of the difference between description, association, and causation in statistical interpretation, especially when reviewing automated explanations.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in the analysis of data and suggests possible feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures, and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Interpretation under 6.3 becomes more closely linked to upstream process quality. When AI-generated explanations expose inconsistencies, unexplained shifts, metadata gaps, or presentational weaknesses, the employee would be expected to feed those findings back into collection, processing, and presentation practices. This creates a stronger loop between output interpretation and methodological improvement.

gaps.justification: The current activity includes suggesting feedback to methods and procedures, but not using issues detected during AI-assisted interpretation as structured evidence for process improvement.
gaps.name: AI-informed quality feedback
gaps.description: Ability to translate issues identified in AI-generated narratives or visualizations into actionable feedback on data production, metadata quality, and presentation methods.

gaps.justification: Because automated explanation quality depends heavily on metadata and production context, the employee must better understand how upstream process choices shape downstream interpretability.
gaps.name: Metadata and process-to-output linkage
gaps.description: Knowledge of how collection, processing, editing, compilation, and presentation decisions affect the quality and explainability of final statistical outputs.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Provides data and assistance to users, within and outside Statistics Canada.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: User assistance will increasingly involve explaining outputs that have been prepared or summarized with AI support, clarifying what is machine-generated versus analyst-confirmed, and helping users interpret visualizations and narratives appropriately. This broadens the assistance function from providing data to mediating understanding of AI-assisted outputs.

gaps.justification: The current activity addresses user support generally, but not user-facing explanation of AI-assisted interpretations or communication of their limitations.
gaps.name: User guidance on AI-assisted outputs
gaps.description: Ability to explain AI-assisted statistical narratives and visualizations to users, including confidence, limitations, caveats, and when further expert interpretation is needed.

gaps.justification: To support external and internal users responsibly, the employee must understand acceptable transparency practices around AI use in analytical communication.
gaps.name: Transparency and accountability in AI-supported communication
gaps.description: Knowledge of how to disclose, document, and communicate the role of AI assistance in interpretation while maintaining trust, clarity, and organizational standards.

affected work-description elements.element: Key Activities - Under guidance, participates in subject matter studies and reviews to support the work of project teams or senior officers.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Subject-matter studies and reviews will now include assessment of AI-generated explanations as inputs to project work. The role will involve checking whether automated narratives reflect the substantive context and whether additional subject-matter analysis is required for sensitive or nuanced topics.

gaps.justification: The current role supports studies and reviews, but the update adds explicit need to supplement AI-generated drafts with domain context and nuance.
gaps.name: Contextual augmentation of automated analysis
gaps.description: Ability to enrich AI-generated interpretations with subject-matter context, caveats, and alternative explanations relevant to economic and social statistics.

affected work-description elements.element: Technical Activities - Communiction - Liaises with other subject matter specialists and users to develop and translate subject-matter requirements into specifications for system development, to suggest improvements to ongoing programs, to negotiate procedural modifications and to establish project plans, priorities and target dates.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Liaison work will increasingly include specifying requirements for AI-assisted interpretation tools, such as accuracy thresholds, review workflows, escalation rules for sensitive outputs, and expectations for explainability and usability. The role may also need to communicate practical issues observed in AI-assisted interpretation to technical and methodological teams.

gaps.justification: The current liaison requirement relates to systems and procedures broadly, but not to defining user and subject-matter requirements for AI-generated analytical products.
gaps.name: AI requirements articulation
gaps.description: Ability to communicate subject-matter and business requirements for AI-assisted interpretation tools, including review needs, content safeguards, and output usability.

gaps.justification: This is a cross-cutting gap because AI review workflows affect system design, analytical production, and user support simultaneously.
gaps.name: Human-in-the-loop AI workflow design
gaps.description: Knowledge of review, escalation, and accountability structures needed to embed AI-generated narratives and analytics into statistical production safely.

affected work-description elements.element: Technical Activities - Writes and presents detailed subject matter and technical concepts, definitions and terms in common terminology in order to explain and clarify divisional systems and applications.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This communication activity now includes translating AI-assisted analytical outputs into plain language while correcting ambiguities or inaccuracies introduced by automation. The employee must be able to preserve conceptual precision when simplifying machine-generated text for broader audiences.

gaps.justification: The current communication expectation covers technical-to-common language translation, but not editing AI-generated prose that may appear fluent while being conceptually weak or imprecise.
gaps.name: Plain-language editing of AI-generated content
gaps.description: Ability to revise AI-generated explanations into clear, accurate, audience-appropriate language without losing statistical meaning or methodological nuance.

affected work-description elements.element: Technical Activities - Writes program information manuals, training packages, monitoring procedures and management reports for use by colleagues, operational staff and management in the development, implementation and assessment of statistical programs.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Documentation duties would expand to include guidance on how AI-assisted interpretations are produced, reviewed, accepted, corrected, and monitored. Management reports and training materials may need to explain controls, responsibilities, and appropriate use cases for AI-generated explanatory content.

gaps.justification: Current documentation expectations do not explicitly include procedural guidance for AI-assisted analytical interpretation and oversight.
gaps.name: Documentation of AI-enabled analytical processes
gaps.description: Ability to document workflows, review criteria, risks, and acceptable practices for the use of AI-generated narratives and visualizations in statistical programs.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of statistical or economic theory and principles and the relevance of their application in a computerized environment, and the methods and techniques of data gathering, statistical estimation and economic modeling.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This knowledge requirement must now extend beyond a general computerized environment to include AI-assisted analytical interpretation environments. The employee must understand how statistical and economic concepts can be misrepresented in automated summaries and how to correct them.

gaps.justification: The current knowledge requirement is broad and relevant, but it does not explicitly include AI-mediated interpretation risks in applying statistical and economic concepts.
gaps.name: Application of statistical theory in AI-mediated interpretation
gaps.description: Knowledge of how core statistical and economic concepts should be represented in AI-assisted narratives, and how to detect distortions or oversimplifications.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of current and emerging economic and social issues relating to the program area in order to identify and assess trends and issues represented by statistical data series.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This requirement gains importance because AI-generated narratives may miss emerging context, overgeneralize, or misread the significance of developments. Human review must anchor interpretation in real-world economic and social conditions.

gaps.justification: The existing work-description already expects awareness of emerging issues, but future work requires stronger ability to use that context to audit and refine automated explanations.
gaps.name: Context-based challenge of automated interpretation
gaps.description: Ability to use current economic and social context to question, refine, or reject AI-generated explanations that are incomplete, implausible, or insufficiently nuanced.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 4. Knowledge of specialized fields - Knowledge of the socio-economic concepts and methods to assess the validity of collected and processed data, the output from computer applications, the validity of database contents and results from alternative manipulations of data.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: The phrase 'output from computer applications' now extends materially to AI-generated narratives, visualizations, and analytical suggestions. Validity assessment must therefore include not only numeric outputs but also machine-produced explanatory content derived from them.

gaps.justification: The current requirement supports assessment of computerized outputs, but not specifically the validity of generated explanatory text and visualization narratives.
gaps.name: Validation of generated analytical content
gaps.description: Knowledge of methods for checking whether AI-generated explanatory content is faithful to source data, metadata, and validated results.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 5. Contextual knowledge - Knowledge of the divisional mandate, objectives, programs, policies and activities to adhere to the various statistical and administrative practices and procedures involved in the collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation of statistical data.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This contextual knowledge must now be applied to the governance of AI-assisted interpretation and explanation. The employee will need to ensure that the use of AI in explanatory outputs remains aligned with divisional standards, approved practices, and public communication expectations.

gaps.justification: This is a systemic gap because governance expectations affect all activities involving AI-assisted interpretation, communication, and documentation.
gaps.name: AI governance in statistical production
gaps.description: Knowledge of organizational policies, quality standards, and governance expectations governing the use of AI tools in statistical interpretation and explanation.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 5. Contextual knowledge - Knowledge of the Statistics Act and other pertinent acts such as the Corporate Returns Act and Income Tax Act,  and of Statistics Canada policies  to ensure understanding and application in the collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation of data.  The position must have a particular awareness of the Statistics and Privacy Acts with respect to the security and confidentiality of data to ensure their own actions are in  compliance.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: AI-assisted interpretation raises additional compliance considerations, especially where prompts, generated narratives, or visual summaries may inadvertently expose sensitive information or reproduce disclosive detail. The role must therefore apply legal and policy obligations to AI-supported explanatory work, not only to raw data handling.

gaps.justification: The current requirement addresses confidentiality and compliance broadly, but AI-assisted narrative generation introduces new risk channels in prompt content, generated text, and visual explanation.
gaps.name: Privacy and confidentiality controls for AI-assisted outputs
gaps.description: Knowledge of how confidentiality, privacy, and statutory obligations apply to the use of AI tools in generating and refining explanatory narratives and visualizations.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 6. Research and analysis - Analyzes changes in procedures, methodology, computer technology and administrative services to determine the effect on data output, products and services.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: The employee will now need to analyze the effect of AI-assisted interpretation technologies on analytical products and services, including changes to quality, speed, consistency, risk, and user understanding.

gaps.justification: The current analytical expectation includes computer technology changes generally, but not specific evaluation of AI impacts on interpretation quality and service delivery.
gaps.name: Assessment of AI impact on analytical products
gaps.description: Ability to assess how AI-assisted interpretation affects quality, consistency, timeliness, accessibility, and risk in statistical outputs and user services.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 6. Research and analysis - Assesses and determines the impact and the constraints on results of the different concepts, definitions and conditions under which the data was collected, processed and stored.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: This analytical responsibility becomes more prominent because AI-generated explanations can overlook the constraints embedded in concepts, definitions, and data production conditions. The role must ensure those constraints are explicitly reintroduced into interpretation.

gaps.justification: Current analysis of conceptual and production constraints is relevant, but future work requires stronger skill in injecting those constraints into review of AI-generated explanatory text.
gaps.name: Constraint-aware interpretation review
gaps.description: Ability to identify where AI-generated explanations fail to reflect conceptual definitions, collection conditions, processing limitations, or comparability constraints, and to correct them.

affected work-description elements.element: Skills - 6. Research and analysis - Analyzes current collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures to ascertain their relevancy and to propose changes or alternative systems.
affected work-description elements.element update reasoning: Presentation methods now include AI-supported narrative and visualization generation. The employee would help assess whether these methods improve interpretability and accessibility, and where alternative processes or controls are needed.

gaps.justification: The existing requirement includes presentation methods, but future-state presentation increasingly includes generated explanatory content that requires dedicated evaluation criteria.
gaps.name: Evaluation criteria for AI-enabled presentation methods
gaps.description: Knowledge of quality criteria for AI-assisted narratives and visualizations, including accuracy, interpretability, accessibility, transparency, and appropriateness for release context.
